item.title: [Yardbarker] Andrew Friedman: Dodgers Will ‘Spend A Lot Of Time’ Looking Into Offensive Struggles
item.dc:creator: Blake Williams

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers’ offense was inconsistent throughout the 2026 season, ultimately leading to their downfall in October.
During the postseason, the Dodgers hit just .195/.267/.323 with nine home runs, 25 runs scored, 22 RBI and a 63 wRC+. They struggled with runners in scoring position, did not slug consistently, and didn’t draw walks at their usual rate.
The Dodgers also had similar issues from July through August, and after turning things around in September against weaker opponents, those issues resurfaced at the worst time.
“That’s something we have to wrap our arms around more,” Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman said of the offensive struggles. “Obviously, throughout the latter part of the year, it was stuff we were talking about and trying to put our finger on.
“And in a lot of ways, it’s a little bit of a game of whack-a-mole, where it can be one thing for some period of time, and then it’s something else, and then it’s something else. Sometimes it’s noise, and sometimes it’s real. And what’s important for us is to be able to sift out the noise and isolate what’s real and what things we can improve upon.
“We’ll spend a lot of time really focusing on that in the offseason. Hitting is really hard, and pitchers make adjustments. In a lot of ways, a lot of the rules are designed for the run prevention side to have a real advantage. And so, so much of our focus has been: how do we try to combat that on the run creation side?
“I think there are ways that we can get better. And even if we were coming off a consistent great year, our mindset would be, how do we get better? But we’ll definitely spend a lot of time trying to wrap our arms around it and figuring out what is actionable and what things we can improve going forward.”
The Dodgers’ offense was also an issue in the 2025 postseason, but they still won the World Series thanks to their pitching staff and timely home runs.
Given the Dodgers have the oldest position player group in MLB, it begs the question of whether the group is just declining, if they’re tired by the end of the season, or if it’s not related to age at all and it’s just some of the randomness of baseball showing up at inopportune times.
“I don’t know the answer,” Friedman said. “I think it’s a good question. It very well could be we need to be more aggressive on the rest side of things, just proactively.
“But there’s a lot of different theories. You could ask me to argue passionately one path or another, and I could do it. Which gets at that it’s very muddied. There’s not a very clear answer.
“So as we’re kind of wrapping our arms around this, we’re going to try to take what we can and improve going forward. And what that means, we don’t know yet.”
The age of the roster being the primary factor for their struggles is a leading theory among fans and analysts. The Dodgers were bullied by fastballs in October, which relates to their lack of elite bat speed as a unit.
If it’s an age issue, that’s a real concern for the Dodgers, given that it would be unrealistic to get significantly younger in a single offseason. Will Smith, Freddie Freeman, Tommy Edman, Mookie Betts, Max Muncy, Teoscar Hernández and Shohei Ohtani are all in their 30s and will be under contract for at least the 2027 season.
Although there is at least some correlation with age, Friedman isn’t ready to say that’s the main reason for their offensive issues.
“I mean, there have been some guys who are older who have finished really strong,” Friedman said. “So I don’t think it’s as easy as to paint it with that broad of a stroke.”
The Dodgers don’t have many paths to upgrade their offense, either. Second base seems to be the primary spot they can upgrade while moving Edman into a utility role.
Josue De Paula also seems destined to be the starting left fielder, which should provide an offensive upgrade over Hernández.
But outside of those potential moves, the Dodgers need Ohtani to be healthy, and they need at least a few of Smith, Betts, Freeman and Muncy to hit like they’re capable of, or else the offense is doomed to struggle again in 2027.
A lot of blame has also been placed on hitting coach Robert Van Scoyoc by fans, which is a natural reaction when the offense struggles. However, Friedman said the Dodgers don’t expect to make any changes to their coaching staff.
Along with Van Scoyoc, Aaron Bates also serves as a hitting coach for the Dodgers. But the reality is hitting coaches also make little impact on a club’s offense, and more of the blame lies on the players and front office.

item.title: [Dodgers Way] Dalton Rushing surgery bomb delays possibility of a Dodgers trade but doesn't erase it
item.dc:creator: Katrina Stebbins
item.description: On Wednesday, the Los Angeles Dodgers revealed Dalton Rushing underwent an internal brace procedure on his elbow, sidelining him from catching for approximately nine months. Andrew Friedman said at his postmortem press conference that Rushing could start swinging a bat sooner, but he won't be behind the dish until well into the 2027 season. Luckily, the Dodgers got their scrambling for catching depth out of the way in-season by reacquiring Hunter Feduccia from the Tampa Bay Rays at the trade dea
item.content:encoded:
On Wednesday, the Los Angeles Dodgers revealed Dalton Rushing underwent an internal brace procedure on his elbow, sidelining him from catching for approximately nine months. Andrew Friedman said at his postmortem press conference that Rushing could start swinging a bat sooner, but he won't be behind the dish until well into the 2027 season.
Luckily, the Dodgers got their scrambling for catching depth out of the way in-season by reacquiring Hunter Feduccia from the Tampa Bay Rays at the trade deadline. Although he hit under .200, the Dodgers still preferred him on both of their postseason rosters over Rushing, who was on the IL with elbow inflammation throughout September.
This kills basically any idea that the Dodgers might finally trade Rushing this offseason, unless they're willing to sell very low. But it's still a possibility for the more distant future.
Feduccia fits into the mold of a traditional backup catcher much more neatly than Rushing, who the Dodgers could still fetch a decent return for in a trade when he's healthy.
Of course, the Dodgers would much rather make their roster that much more formidable by having a backup catcher who would be a starter on any other team, but if Feduccia can use Rushing's absence as an opportunity to prove that his bat won't represent a total black hole in the lineup, the Dodgers could be more inclined to let go of Rushing next offseason.
Dodgers catcher Dalton Rushing will be sidelined for nine months
A nine-month recovery timeline would have Rushing back on defense by the end of July — only if all goes according to plan. Even if he's healthy enough to swing a bat before then, opportunities as a pinch-hitter or DH on Shohei Ohtani's off-days will be scarce. The Dodgers could use the rest of the regular season to get Rushing back into a groove behind Will Smith and see if it drives his trade value back up to a point where they're willing to deal him.
The Dodgers would never admit to it outright, but it seems that they've fallen out of love with Rushing. Although concerns about his elbow probably factored into their decision to carry Josue De Paula into the postseason instead, Rushing was very much in that conversation and didn't make the cut.
They could still get a healthy return back for him, too, despite character concerns and injuries. He's too young and controllable, and has too good a pedigree for the Dodgers to give him away for a song.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Dodgers' Dalton Rushing Undergoing Surgery That Will Cost Him Significant Time
item.dc:creator: Aaliyan Mohammed
item.description: Dalton Rushing stepped up big time for the Dodgers while Will Smith was out, but he, too, suffered injuries of his own. Rushing was placed on the injured list with right elbow inflammation in August, but returned in September. However, he was placed back on the injured list with right elbow discomfort. He was left off the postseason roster, and on Wednesday, The Los Angeles Times' Maddie Lee reported that he is undergoing elbow surgery. "Dodgers' Dalton Rushing is undergoing right elbow surgery
item.content:encoded:
Dalton Rushing stepped up big time for the Dodgers while Will Smith was out, but he, too, suffered injuries of his own.
Rushing was placed on the injured list with right elbow inflammation in August, but returned in September. However, he was placed back on the injured list with right elbow discomfort. He was left off the postseason roster, and on Wednesday, The Los Angeles Times' Maddie Lee reported that he is undergoing elbow surgery.
"Dodgers' Dalton Rushing is undergoing right elbow surgery today, per sources," wrote Lee. "It's expected to be a hybrid internal brace procedure. The expected timeline to return to catching full time is 9 months, with a return to hitting well before then."
When he was healthy, Rushing was a solid hitter for the Dodgers, proving why he was once a top prospect in the organization. However, his inability to play behind the plate while he recovers really limits the impact he can make.
It's not like the Dodgers can put him at designated hitter with Shohei Ohtani on the team. Even though he would be able to hit well before he could play as a catcher again, he may only be able to pinch-hit until then.
On top of that, the Dodgers have Smith. Rushing was already going to be pressed for playing time. Overall, the Dodgers will have to make some important decisions with Rushing down the line.
He is a good player, but as long as Smith and Ohtani are on the team, his role will always be limited.

item.content:encoded:
When Dalton Rushing can return to full-time catching for the Dodgers after elbow surgery appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
When news broke that Dalton Rushing suffered a partially torn UCL in his right elbow back in August, fans openly wondered if and when the Los Angeles Dodgers catcher would have surgery to fix it.
At the time, any surgery would have effectively ended his season, leaving LA without a key bat on the bench, so, after deliberation, the team opted for rehab instead, allowing Rushing to remain a pinch-hitting option for another World Series run.
Unfortunately, that World Series berth didn't materialize, and now Rushing will be unable to catch full-time for the next nine months after undergoing right elbow surgery on October 21, which Andrew Freedman revealed to reporters like Maddie Lee of the LA Times during his season-of-season press conference.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
"Dodgers' Dalton Rushing is undergoing right elbow surgery today, per sources," Lee wrote. "It's expected to be a hybrid internal brace procedure. The expected timeline to return to catching full time is 9 months, with a return to hitting well before then."
On paper, the Dodgers' desire to keep Rushing's bat available made sense, as he was a quality performer at times during the season. But the emergence of Josue De Paula as a major league hitter quickly made Rushing irrelevant, to the point where he didn't take a single at-bat against the Atlanta Braves or the Milwaukee Brewers. With his catching return now set for mid-summer, the Dodgers will have to hope reserves like Hunter Feduccia can hold things down behind Will Smith, or that Rushing can find some work at first base to remain a more consistent part of Dave Roberts' offense.
Related: 2 trades Dodgers must make after disappointing NLCS loss to Brewers

item.content:encoded:
Following their disappointing elimination from World Series contention, the Los Angeles Dodgers announced an update on catcher Dalton Rushing.
Rushing, 25, was sidelined for the entire postseason with a partial tear of the ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) in his throwing arm. The Dodgers’ second catcher on the roster tried to play through the injury as a designated hitter but never appeared in the postseason.
Today, the Dodgers announced that Rushing will undergo surgery to address the elbow injury, Maddie Lee of the Los Angeles Times wrote.
“It’s expected to be a hybrid internal brace procedure. The expected timeline to return to catching full time is 9 months, with a return to hitting well before then,” Lee added.
Dalton Rushing’s Boosted Opportunity Derailed by Elbow Injury
The Dodgers’ second-year catcher got a new opportunity as the team’s primary catcher. The team gave him this chance while Will Smith was sidelined with a lingering neck injury that kept the Dodgers’ top catcher out for nearly three months.
Rushing was up for the new challenge. Before suffering the UCL tear, Rushing was batting .245/.335/.475 with 12 home runs and 36 RBIs.
Will Smith would finally return to the Dodgers lineup on Sept. 1. Meanwhile, the Dodgers’ depth at catcher remained limited as Rushing became unable to play defense.
The nine-month recovery period for Dalton Rushing goes in line with a return to catching in late July 2027. A return to batting will be significantly earlier for the 25-year-old.
Offseason Surgery ‘Not on the Table’ For Shohei Ohtani
LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA – OCTOBER 15: Shohei Ohtani #17 of the Los Angeles Dodgers reacts after striking out against the Milwaukee Brewers during the fifth inning in game four of the National League Championship Series at Dodger Stadium on October 15, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Sean M. Haffey/Getty Images)
Throughout the Dodgers’ 2026 season, the health status of superstar Shohei Ohtani was an ongoing conversation. For the first time since joining the franchise in 2024, the team sent Ohtani to the 15-day injured list at the end of the regular season.
The designation was due to right biceps inflammation, left knee discomfort, and a neck issue. The biceps and knee injuries surfaced earlier in the season, leading manager Dave Roberts to give him regular days off.
As the Dodgers won’t be the World Series Champion for the first time since 2023, the option for surgery to address the lingering setbacks is “not on the table,” says Dodgers president Andrew Friedman.
The Dodgers president also added that he fully expects Ohtani “to pitch next year.”
The 32-year-old was shut down from pitching in early July. In the limited opportunity on the mound, Ohtani finished the 2026 season as a pitcher with an 8-2 record, 1.79 ERA, and 0.95 WHIP across 85.2 innings.
After back-to-back 50-home-run, 100-RBI seasons, the injuries limited Ohtani to 30 home runs and 81 RBIs in 2026.
The Dodgers superstar said he “definitely” plans on pitching next season.
“And looking forward to having a better season next year,” Ohtani added.

item.title: [Los Angeles Times] Commentary: Enough is enough. The Dodgers must stop letting Shohei Ohtani pitch
item.dc:creator: Bill Plaschke
item.description: - Click here to listen to this article - Shohei Ohtani’s two-way brilliance helped the Dodgers win two World Series titles and become a global draw, but his age and injuries are raising questions about the cost of pitching. - Ohtani says he plans to pitch next season, leaving the Dodgers with a difficult choice: find a way to manage his workload or consider a future without him. As they head into an offseason of overdue rest and roster reshaping, the Dodgers really only face one obstacle. But it
item.content:encoded:
- Click here to listen to this article
- Shohei Ohtani’s two-way brilliance helped the Dodgers win two World Series titles and become a global draw, but his age and injuries are raising questions about the cost of pitching.
- Ohtani says he plans to pitch next season, leaving the Dodgers with a difficult choice: find a way to manage his workload or consider a future without him.
As they head into an offseason of overdue rest and roster reshaping, the Dodgers really only face one obstacle.
But it’s a $700-million obstacle. It’s a 5,400-mile obstacle. It’s an obstacle whose gravitas can be found in everything from international sponsorships to stadium tours, an obstacle with expansive implications and crushing consequences.
The Dodgers have a Shohei Ohtani problem.
He is their best player… and their biggest pain.
He is insanely charming… and unrelentingly stubborn.
Dalton Rushing, who filled in for an injured Will Smith this season, had two stints on the injured list with a flexor strain in his right forearm, along with the UCL tear.
He has derived his worldwide popularity from his ability to hit and pitch with equal prowess, a deft duality unmatched in the history of baseball. This ability has helped earn him four MVP awards and status as the unofficial greatest player ever.
And, yeah, it’s made him very rich, setting him up to sign a 10-year, $700-million contract with the Dodgers based on the notion that he was not one, but two players, an All-Star hitter and an All-Star pitcher.
Three seasons later, he’s earned every penny, leading the Dodgers to two World Series championships while turning them into a global money machine, transforming this once staid organization into one of the most popular sports franchises in the world.
But, he’s changing. His body is changing. His skills are changing. He’s 32, with 13 seasons of professional baseball burdening his lumbering 6-foot-4 frame, and part of his game is slowly disintegrating under the weight.
The problem is his pitching. It’s hurting him. It’s distracting him. It’s exhausting him. His attempts to fix it on the mound led to a badly broken swing at the plate that may have caused the Dodgers to fail in their attempt at a three-peat.
And enough is enough.
This past season offered unassailable proof that Shohei Ohtani can no longer serve as both a full-time hitter and full-time pitcher. The Dodgers have no choice but to act on this truth and make a decision that is not only best for this team, but the long-term future of the organization.
They need to pull him off the pitching mound permanently. And if he insists on continuing this detrimental charade, they need to seriously consider trading him.
The Dodgers, after falling short of a three-peat in the NLCS, will look a little different next year. But is this the end of an era for the team?
Yes, yes, of course, trading Shohei Ohtani might be the dumbest move since the Boston Red Sox traded Babe Ruth. And, don’t forget, Ohtani has a no-trade clause that places him squarely in charge of his future here.
But at some point, if he insists on pitching despite the damage it is doing to his hitting and thus the entire team’s offense, the Dodgers may need to discuss other options with him.
Like, do what’s best for the team or take a hike.
The Dodgers, of course, are saying no such thing. Publicly, despite the hell he put them through, they are still backing him as a pitcher.
”I’m not only expecting him to pitch, we’re excited about him pitching,” Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman told reporters Wednesday at his postseason news conference. “The value of it is incredible, and so now it is incumbent on all of us to figure out the best way to do it.”
That’s going to require a lot of figuring, and it comes down to one seven-month task.
“How do we manage through a long season and have him at his best going into October...that’s a challenge,” Friedman said.
Challenge? A better word might be, “Impossibility.”
For all of his optimism, Friedman hedged his bet when asked if it was possible for a pitcher at Ohtani’s age to survive an entire season and postseason as a two-way player.
“I don’t know the answer to that,” he said.
The answer, obviously, would be for Ohtani to walk into Friedman’s office this winter and tell him he’s done pitching and ready to win more MVP awards as a full-time hitter.
But so far, that’s not happening. That’s not even close to happening.
As of his locker-room interview immediately after the Game 4 sweeping by the Milwaukee Brewers last week, Ohtani still insists on pitching.
When asked a direct question about whether he planned to pitch next season, his answer was firm.
“Yes, definitely,” he told reporters through interpreter Will Ireton. “And looking forward to having a better season next year.”
He was also quite clear that he was unhappy ending the season off the mound, and will work on whatever adjustments are required to make sure that doesn’t happen again.
Major League Baseball is heading toward a turbulent offseason. There are four major things the Dodgers must address if they want to get back to the top.
“Not quite satisfied with how things shaped up on the pitching side at the end of the year,” he said. “This year, I haven’t pitched and I haven’t pitched in the postseason. You know, I haven’t been able to really come to grips in terms of what I’ve learned overall this season. It’s something that I’m going to kind of go back to the drawing board in terms of treatment, training program. and see what I can come up with for next season.”
Alas, there is no treatment for age. There is no training program for too many innings. There is nothing he can do to change the downward trajectory of his pitching career enough to save his hitting.
It’s not that he can’t pitch. In 14 starts this year he was 8-2 with a 1.79 ERA. If he devoted all of his time to pitching, he could easily win a couple of Cy Young awards to complement his four MVPs.
But since his second elbow surgery in 2023, he has yet to both hit and pitch in a full season. He strictly batted in 2024 while rehabbing from the surgery, then only started 14 games at the end of the 2025 season while the Dodgers slowly returned him to the mound.
Then came this season, which began with Ohtani openly pursuing a Cy Young Award while pitching at a Cy Young level.
But around midseason, his body began breaking down, the left knee, the right biceps, all of it hurting worse than he’d ever admit. He stopped pitching July 3 but kept working to return to the mound even while his hitting was declining from the constant effort.
The Dodgers should have shut him down in July and not allowed him back on the field in any capacity until he was fully healed. But they bowed to the wishes of their superstar, who insisted on continuing his unicorn quest even though it was clear that age and wear were finally taking its toll.
It was an organizational mistake that arguably cost them their season. He was finally pulled off the bullpen mound and yanked out of the lineup and placed on the injured list in September, but by then it was too late. Not only did he not pitch again, he stopped hitting, batting .192 in the postseason with four singles and a last-gasp home run.
The Dodgers aren’t the Dodgers without Ohtani creating chaos at the top of the order. They had won the previous two World Series titles on the shoulders of Ohtani the hitter, not Ohtani the pitcher.
Remember, he didn’t even pitch in the 2024 postseason, and in the 2025 postseason he recorded a 4.43 ERA in four starts, and yet they won both World Series championships
This current version of the Dodgers have proven they don’t need his pitching, but desperately need his hitting.
Now they need to convince him of that, and it won’t be easy. Being a two-way player is how he made his fortune. Being a two-way player is how he views his very identity.
Surely Ohtani saw this coming. His own father hinted at it in an open letter about his son after last season.
Shohei Ohtani showed the world a glimpse of his game-breaking abilities in Game 4 of the NLCS, but it was too little, too late for a Dodgers team that needs him healthy to challenge for a World Series title.
“ I believe the time will eventually come when he’ll focus on either pitching or hitting,” said Toru in a statement. “ If he can’t pitch anymore, I think he could do well as an outfielder. With practice, I’m sure he could handle it.”
Hmmm. The Dodgers could need a left fielder if they trade Teoscar Hernández as expected. Maybe Ohtani will accept surrendering the mound if he is handed a spot in the outfield?
No matter what happens, something has to happen, because what’s happening now is not working.
Shohei Ohtani as a two-way player has become a one-way ticket to disaster, and if he’s not willing to accept that reality, maybe he should be offered a one-way ticket out of Los Angeles.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Dodgers’ Dalton Rushing undergoing elbow surgery, leaving 2027 role unclear
item.dc:creator: Jack Harris
item.description: Shohei Ohtani avoided surgery after his injury-plagued 2026 season. Dodgers backup catcher Dalton Rushing, however, wasn't so lucky. Rushing was set to undergo an internal brace procedure on Wednesday to address the damaged ligament in his right throwing elbow, according to multiple sources with knowledge of the situation. The operation will come with a nine-month timeline to return to full catching duties, as the Los Angeles Times first reported, but the expectation is that he could be ready as
item.content:encoded:
Shohei Ohtani avoided surgery after his injury-plagued 2026 season.
Dodgers backup catcher Dalton Rushing, however, wasn't so lucky.
Rushing was set to undergo an internal brace procedure on Wednesday to address the damaged ligament in his right throwing elbow, according to multiple sources with knowledge of the situation.
The operation will come with a nine-month timeline to return to full catching duties, as the Los Angeles Times first reported, but the expectation is that he could be ready as a hitter by the beginning of next season.
Rushing initially hurt his elbow at the beginning of August, while playing catch in the outfield before the start of a game. He spent much of the final two months of the regular season on the injured list, returning for only six days in early September before going down again when he suffered a setback in his throwing progression.
Rushing was healthy enough to be activated for hitting-only duties during the final week of the regular season. However, he did not make the team's postseason roster, bypassed by rookie sensation Josue De Paula as the team's left-handed bench bat in October.
Now, more uncertainty awaits Rushing, who is two years removed from his debut as one of the club's top prospects.
For all the strides he took in his second MLB campaign –– batting .246 with 12 home runs and 36 RBIs in 80 games, including an extended stint in June and July as the fill-in starter behind the plate during Will Smith's neck injury –– his place in the team's long-term plans remains unclear.
Rushing's surgery likely opens a pathway for Hunter Feduccia to begin next season in the backup catcher role, where he impressed as Rushing's replacement down the stretch this year.
Where Rushing will fit into the early-season roster is unknown.
Though he could still offer an option off the bench with his bat, there might be few opportunities for regular playing time with Shohei Ohtani entrenched as the designated hitter and Freddie Freeman at first base.
It's all just another setback for the 25-year-old slugger, who has yet to truly flourish at the big-league level.

item.title: [abc7.com] Where 2026 ranks among best World Series matchups since 2000
item.dc:creator: David Schoenfield
item.description: This year's World Series will have a tough act to follow. Not only was the 2025 World Series between the Los Angeles Dodgers and Toronto Blue Jays the first seven-game affair since 2019, but it featured an 18-inning game and then a Game 7 that might have been the greatest baseball game ever played. The good news is we're guaranteed that a long-starved fanbase will get to celebrate in 2026. The Milwaukee Brewers, coming off their impressive and dynamic four-game sweep of the Dodgers in the NLCS,
item.content:encoded:
This year's World Series will have a tough act to follow. Not only was the 2025 World Series between the Los Angeles Dodgers and Toronto Blue Jays the first seven-game affair since 2019, but it featured an 18-inning game and then a Game 7 that might have been the greatest baseball game ever played.
The good news is we're guaranteed that a long-starved fanbase will get to celebrate in 2026. The Milwaukee Brewers, coming off their impressive and dynamic four-game sweep of the Dodgers in the NLCS, are in the Fall Classic for the first time since 1982 and seek the first championship in franchise history, looking to put an exclamation point on their season after leading the majors with 103 wins.
The Tampa Bay Rays were a 1998 expansion franchise and reached the World Series in 2008 and 2020 (the shortened season during the COVID-19 pandemic) but are seeking their first title as well. Young power hitter Junior Caminero and unheralded staff ace Drew Rasmussen lead the way as the Rays look to finally cash in after making the playoffs six times in the past eight seasons.
The Brewers and Rays led their respective leagues in wins, always a bonus for those who want the best teams in the World Series. Of course, a lot of attention will be given to the small-market aspect of the matchup, as the cloud of the lockout looms in the offseason.
Let's rank all the World Series since 2000 to see where Brewers-Rays fits in. This ranking is based on hype, the quality of the teams and their star power heading into the World Series. It's not a ranking of the quality of the World Series itself, although we're going to include a grade on that for each matchup. Let's get to it.
The Yankees were back in the World Series for the sixth time in eight years, and the Marlins had rebuilt after their fire sale following their World Series title in 1997. Trust me when I say that nobody wanted the Yankees in the World Series yet again. And the Marlins were merely a 91-win wild-card team. Most notably, however, both teams had spoiled the ultimate World Series by knocking off the Cubs and Red Sox -- before either team had overcome its curse -- in Game 7s in the LCS.
Actual World Series: C. The Marlins won Game 4 in 12 innings, when Yankees manager Joe Torre inexplicably failed to use reliever Mariano Rivera, and then 23-year-old Josh Beckett tossed a five-hit shutout in Game 6.
In an all-wild-card series, the fifth-seeded Rangers had won 90 games and the sixth-seeded Diamondbacks won only 84, making this the lowest combined win total in World Series history (for full seasons). The Rangers were going for their first World Series title, so there was that, and there were some fun hitters -- Corey Seager, the red-hot Adolis Garcia (who had just driven in 15 runs in the ALCS) and Corbin Carroll -- but it was a soft matchup on paper.
Actual World Series: D-. The series turned on Seager's tying two-run homer off Paul Sewald in the bottom of the ninth of Game 1, which Garcia then won with a home run in the 11th. There wasn't a single lead change after that, and three of those games were blowouts.
This was the Cardinals team that got hot in September and clinched a wild-card spot on the final day of the season when the Braves blew a lead in the ninth inning and lost in extra innings. St. Louis certainly had star power with the likes of Albert Pujols, Lance Berkman and Matt Holliday but had won a World Series fairly recently (2006), and the Rangers had just been there the year before.
Actual World Series: A. The first two games were one-run games, including the Rangers pulling out a victory with two runs in the ninth. In Game 3, Pujols blasted a record-tying three home runs. Game 6 was the David Freese Game -- perhaps the single most exciting baseball game ever played. Game 7 was a bit of an anticlimactic 6-2 Cardinals win.
The second-lowest combined win total in World Series history featured two wild-card teams that won fewer than 90 games. The Royals were at least a good story -- in the playoffs for the first time since winning the World Series in 1985 -- and had gone 8-0 in the AL playoffs, including an epic win over the A's in the wild-card game. The Giants, however, had just won the World Series in 2010 and 2012, and this team didn't seem nearly as good as those two.
Actual World Series: B-. Five of the games were blowouts, but it did at least go seven. It'll be remembered for Madison Bumgarner's historic performance: a shutout in Game 5 (the last complete game shutout in World Series history) and then five scoreless innings of relief in Game 7, getting Salvador Perez to pop out with the tying run on third to end it.
The Red Sox were only three years removed from breaking the Curse of the Bambino in 2004, so although they were still a star-laden team with David Ortiz, Manny Ramirez and scrappy rookie Dustin Pedroia, they were no longer as interesting. The Rockies were a fun story, winning 14 of their final 15 games, including beating the Padres in a tiebreaker, just to win a wild-card spot. Then they went 7-0 in the NL playoffs and had won 21 of 22 entering the World Series.
Actual World Series: F.A dud. Two of the games were one-run games, but this goes down as one of the least memorable World Series of all time, with a forgettable four-game sweep.
The Tigers were the story of the season. They had lost 119 games three years before and 91 just the previous year. With rookie starter Justin Verlander winning 17 games, they led the AL Central most of the season -- only to lose their final five games and squeak into the playoffs as a wild-card team. The Cardinals won a weak NL Central with only 83 wins -- although they at least had Pujols at his absolute peak (.331/.431/.671, 49 home runs). Both teams hadn't won a World Series in a couple of decades: 1982 for the Cardinals, 1984 for the Tigers. Plus, it did feature two of the original 16 franchises.
Actual World Series: F. The Cardinals won one game in the bottom of the eighth, but it was otherwise a blur of nothing, most characterized by several fielding miscues by Tigers pitchers. David Eckstein won MVP honors without hitting a home run and while driving in only four runs.
The Braves were back in the World Series for the first time since 1999 -- they had made 12 playoff appearances in the intervening years without making it to the Fall Classic. Still, this was the weakest of the Atlanta playoff teams of recent vintage, winning only 88 games and missing Ronald Acuña Jr. for the playoffs. The Astros, meanwhile, were back in the World Series for the third time in five years -- but the first time since the 2017 sign-stealing scandal had broken in November 2019. Let's just say not everyone wanted them there.
Actual World Series: D. This was a weird World Series. The Braves ended up going with two bullpen games (who remembers that Dylan Lee and Tucker Davidson started?) after Charlie Morton broke a leg in Game 1. Astros starters kept getting knocked out early (the only starter to go more than five innings for either team was Max Fried in the finale). Four of the games were blowouts.
The Giants were back after winning in 2010, and the Tigers were back for the first time since 2006, featuring Triple Crown winner Miguel Cabrera and a strong 1-2 punch in the rotation with Verlander and Max Scherzer. This was also the last World Series with that season's MVP winners until Aaron Judge and Shohei Ohtani in 2024, with Cabrera and Buster Posey.
Actual World Series: D-. A boring sweep. Pablo Sandoval did hit three home runs in Game 1, but there were two shutouts and chilly weather in Detroit made the final two games unbearable.
This one did feature the two best teams from the regular season (both won 97 games), the last time before this year that we had that happen in a full season. It was also a classic original-16 matchup, although we had seen this in 2004 -- plus, both teams had won recently (2007 for Boston, 2011 for St. Louis). These were veteran teams, with Ortiz leading the Red Sox and the Cardinals featuring four .300 hitters, plus Carlos Beltran, who hit .296 and led the team in home runs.
Actual World Series: C+. Ortiz was absolutely locked in, hitting .688/.760/1.188 with two home runs and eight walks. The Cardinals were so scared of him by Game 6 that they intentionally walked him three times -- with two of those helping lead to rallies and a 6-1 Red Sox victory in the final game.
This one could be No. 25 -- it was during the pandemic, after all, and it was played at a neutral site in a half-empty stadium for social distancing reasons. But it was a great matchup between the teams with the best records in each league, albeit over the shortened 60-game season. You had Mookie Betts and Clayton Kershaw and Randy Arozarena in the midst of one of the best postseasons ever, plus the small-market Rays trying to beat the big-market Dodgers.
Actual World Series: C+. Because teams were allowed an expanded roster of 28 players, it was a parade of relievers -- but there were some fun games, including a bonkers ending to Game 4 and then Rays manager Kevin Cash's controversial decision to remove Blake Snell in Game 6, which backfired in a big way.
Maybe this should rate higher. After all, at the time, the White Sox were trying to break a World Series drought going back to 1917 and the Astros, born in 1962, had never won. But the White Sox's drought never had the same nationwide interest as the ones for the Cubs or Red Sox (fair or not) and these weren't particularly interesting teams. The White Sox were very good -- they won 99 games -- but lacked star power, with Paul Konerko their biggest name (Frank Thomas was on the team that year but played only 34 games and was injured for the playoffs). The Astros had Yankees transplants Roger Clemens and Andy Pettitte, but their two longtime stars, Jeff Bagwell and Craig Biggio, were at the end of their careers (Bagwell, in his final season, was relegated to DH and pinch-hitting duties).
Actual World Series: C. It's hard to give a sweep a decent grade, but all four games were exciting, including Scott Podsednik's walk-off home run in Game 2 (after not hitting a home run all season) and Geoff Blum's go-ahead home run in the 14th inning to win Game 3.
The Phillies were back in the World Series for the first time since 1993 -- and hadn't won since 1980. They featured a powerful offense with Chase Utley, Ryan Howard, Jimmy Rollins and Pat Burrell. The Rays were maybe the unlikeliest World Series team ever: In their 10 previous years of existence, they had not only never had a winning season but had lost at least 90 games in each one. They won 97 games that year behind rookie Evan Longoria and power-hitting first baseman Carlos Peña, with speedsters Carl Crawford and B.J. Upton in the outfield.
Actual World Series: D+. Three games were decided by one run, but it was a pretty uneventful World Series. The lasting memory is the cold and rain in Philly that forced the midgame postponement of Game 5, the only time that has happened in World Series history. The game was suspended in the sixth inning and resumed two days later.
A Subway Series -- the first since the Yankees and Brooklyn Dodgers met in 1956 -- was certainly fun for the Big Apple, but it was less fun for the rest of the country (it drew the worst TV ratings at the time). The Yankees were going for a third straight World Series and had officially become the Evil Empire by that point. To make it even worse, they weren't even that good that season, winning only 87 games. The Mets were back in the World Series for the first time since 1986. There was certainly plenty of star power all around with the likes of Derek Jeter, Roger Clemens and Mike Piazza.
Actual World Series: C+. It was a tight-fought five-game series with all games decided by two runs or fewer. The turning point was the bottom of the ninth of Game 1, when the Yankees tied it off Armando Benitez and went on to win in 12 innings. Game 2 featured the infamous Clemens-Piazza bat-throwing incident, and the Yankees won the clincher with two runs in the ninth off a tired Al Leiter.
I know, the Astros ... again. Boo. But this was an absolute powerhouse of a team with 106 wins and stars such asYordan Alvarez (1.019 OPS) and Verlander (18-4, 1.75 ERA), plus the old standbys Jose Altuve and Alex Bregman. The Phillies, meanwhile, snuck in as a wild-card team for their first playoff trip since 2011 but were an immensely entertaining team with Bryce Harper, Kyle Schwarber& Co., as well as a passionate fanbase cheering them on.
Actual World Series: C. The Phillies won 6-5 in Game 1 on J.T. Realmuto's home run in the 10th inning. They took a 2-1 series lead, but then their bats died. Astros pitchers tossed a combined no-hitter to even the series, and Houston won the final two games 3-2 and 4-1, with Alvarez's three-run blast in Game 6 the deciding blow.
The Brewers' drought is the big narrative here as they try to finally cash in after their past decade of success, but we're still getting the 103-win Brewers facing the 98-win Rays, the best combined win total in the World Series since the Astros and Dodgers in 2017. (Not to mention we get a first-time winner no matter the outcome.) The Brewers aren't your conventional powerhouse team -- relying on speed, defense, timely hitting and a dominant bullpen -- but they do have one of the biggest stars of the 2026 season in Jacob Misiorowski, plus a rising star in young Jackson Chourio. The Rays might lack big names, although Junior Caminero is just the second player with two 40-homer seasons by age 22, and like the Brewers, they're trying to finally win it all after years of success.
Actual World Series: To be determined.
The Royals proved their 2014 World Series appearance was no fluke, winning 95 games with a better team that included trade deadline additions Ben Zobrist and Johnny Cueto. The Mets won the NL East behind a young, powerful rotation that featured Matt Harvey, Noah Syndergaard and Jacob deGrom. It was a fun matchup of teams trying to avoid lengthy title droughts -- 30 years for the Royals, 29 for the Mets.
Actual World Series: C+. It went only five games, but the Royals won the opener in 14 innings, won Game 5 with a three-run eighth inning and then won the clincher in 12 innings -- after Mets manager Terry Collins' ill-fated decision to leave in Harvey to start the ninth with a 2-0 lead.
This was a super entertaining showdown at the time. The Giants had yet to win a World Series in San Francisco and featured Tim Lincecum ("The Freak," for his small stature and overpowering stuff) and two rookies named Posey and Bumgarner. The Rangers had never won a championship and featured AL MVP Josh Hamilton and veteran DH Vladimir Guerrero. Both teams had pulled off upsets in the LCS, with the Giants beating the Phillies and the Rangers beating the Yankees.
Actual World Series: D. Meh. The Giants won the opener in a blowout as the Rangers made four errors and then tossed shutouts in Games 2 (behind Matt Cain) and 4 (behind Bumgarner). You can test Giants fans by asking them who won World Series MVP honors that year. Answer: Edgar Renteria (he hit .412 with two home runs and six RBIs).
Remember, this happened before the sign-stealing scandal changed how we view this era of the Astros. They had won 107 games behind the pitching duo of Verlander and Gerrit Cole and four players who mashed 30-plus home runs (which didn't even include Alvarez, a rookie that year). The Nationals were a wild-card team that had overcome a 19-31 season start to win 93 games and featured a starting pitching trio of Scherzer, Stephen Strasburg and Patrick Corbin (and 20-year-old sensation Juan Soto, who hit 34 home runs).
Actual World Series: B-. It went seven games -- the road team would win all seven -- although five of the games weren't close. The best game was the last one: The Nationals went ahead 3-2 in the seventh inning on Anthony Rendon's home run and then Howie Kendrick's go-ahead home run just inside the right-field foul pole.
This matchup began with a lot of hype: Shohei Ohtani, coming off his all-time game in the NLCS in which he hit three home runs and struck out 10 batters as the starting pitcher, against Vladimir Guerrero Jr., who had hit .442 with six home runs through the first two rounds of the playoffs. The Dodgers were looking to become the first team with back-to-back titles since the 2000 Yankees and the first NL team since the 1976 Reds. The Blue Jays were back in the World Series for the first time since Joe Carter walked off the Phillies in 1993. Dodgers manager Dave Roberts stirred things up after the NLCS when he said during the postgame celebration, "Let's get four more wins and really ruin baseball" -- a reference to the criticism of the Dodgers' high payroll.
Actual World Series: A+. The Dodgers won Game 3 in 18 innings on Freddie Freeman's walk-off home run, which followed an unlikely four-inning relief performance from Will Klein, the last guy on the Dodgers' staff. The Dodgers went back to Toronto trailing 3-2 but won Game 6 behind Yoshinobu Yamamoto and a crazy game-ending double play.
Game 7 featured two future Hall of Famers starting in Ohtani and Max Scherzer, more on-the-edge-of-your-seat plays than any game in World Series history, Miguel Rojas' unlikely home run in the ninth to tie it, as well as Will Smith's go-ahead one in the 11th -- and finally, Yamamoto pitching in relief to close out the game by inducing a double play with two runners on to win it for the Dodgers. It wasn't quite the greatest World Series overall, but two all-time games made it a classic.
The Angels, who joined the majors in 1961, were making their first World Series appearance, while the Giants, in the Bay Area since 1958, were trying to win their first title since moving from New York. You had Barry Bonds at the height of his unstoppable powers -- and trying to erase his own postseason demons -- while the Angels had a loaded lineup (Troy Glaus, Tim Salmon, Garret Anderson), the Rally Monkey and those deafening ThunderStix (let us pray they never return).
Actual World Series: A. Bonds was a beast, hitting .471/.700/1.294 (yes, that's a 1.994 OPS), but it wasn't enough. This series featured four one-run games, including a wild 11-10 contest and the classic Game 6, when the Angels rallied late from a 5-0 deficit to win 6-5. Game 7 was a drab 4-1 contest (Bonds went a harmless 1-for-3).
The Yankees had missed the playoffs in 2008 for the first time since 1993, so they went out and signed free agents CC Sabathia, Mark Teixeira and A.J. Burnett to add to an already stacked roster that included Jeter, Alex Rodriguez, Robinson Cano, Hideki Matsui, Jorge Posada and Johnny Damon. Whoa. Yes, they were still the Evil Empire. The Phillies, trying to defend their title, had traded for Cliff Lee and then signed Pedro Martinez in July to bolster their rotation.
Actual World Series: C. It could have been a classic battle, but there were no one-run games and Game 6 -- Martinez's final start of his career -- was over early. The crucial contest was Game 4, when the Yankees scored three runs in the ninth off Phillies closer Brad Lidge to win 7-4.
This one presented conflicting emotions. The Yankees were going for an unthinkable fourth straight title, but in the wake of 9/11, there was a "Win it for New York" angle that the Yankees had never encountered. The Diamondbacks, meanwhile, had the big, bad duo of Randy Johnson and Curt Schilling. When asked on the eve of the World Series about the Yankees' mystique and aura, Schilling provided one of the great quips in World Series history: "Mystique and Aura? Those are dancers at a nightclub." The Diamondbacks were not going to be intimidated.
Actual World Series: A+. Four one-run games, including three of the most memorable World Series moments ever: Jeter's Mr. November home run to win Game 4, Scott Brosius' walk-off home run to win Game 5 and then Luis Gonzalez's bloop single to beat the invincible Mariano Rivera in Game 7.
Two of baseball's most historic franchises had never met in a World Series, creating the classic showdown with games in Fenway Park and Dodger Stadium. It doesn't get any better than that. The Red Sox were a 108-win powerhouse -- with AL MVP Mookie Betts leading the way, backed up by J.D. Martinez, who hit .330 with 43 home runs that season. Chris Sale and David Price headlined the rotation. The Dodgers actually had a bit of a down year with 92 wins, but they also weren't lacking in big names, with Manny Machado (a trade deadline acquisition), Yasiel Puig, Matt Kemp, Cody Bellinger and Justin Turner, with Kershaw and rookie Walker Buehler on the pitching side.
Actual World Series: C-. A letdown. The first two games in Fenway were cold and windy. Game 3 was an 18-inning affair -- the longest in World Series history -- but was more of a slog than a game to remember. Game 4 was the best of the series as the Red Sox rallied with nine runs over the final three innings to win 9-6.
This series had it all: dominant teams (both won over 100 games), long World Series title droughts (never for the Astros, 1988 for the Dodgers) and superstars galore (Altuve, Verlander, Carlos Correa, Kershaw, Seager, Bellinger, Yu Darvish). We didn't know at the time that both franchises were just kicking off 100-win dynasties -- let alone what the Astros were doing behind the scenes -- but the anticipation level was off the charts for the first matchup of 100-win teams in the World Series since 1970.
Actual World Series: A-. Game 1, with a start-time temperature of 103 degrees at Dodger Stadium, was a Kershaw 11-strikeout gem. The Astros tied Game 2 in the ninth on Marwin Gonzalez's home run off Kenley Jansen (1.32 ERA that season), both teams scored twice in the 10th, the Astros scored twice in the 11th on George Springer's home run and held on for a 7-6 win. Game 4 featured a five-run rally in the ninth by the Dodgers to win. Game 5 was completely bananas, with the Astros finally winning 13-12 in 10 innings. Game 7 was a letdown though, as the Astros won a 5-1 snoozer in which they scored five runs off Darvish in the first two innings.
As mentioned, what's not to like? Aside from Ohtani and Judge each playing in their first World Series and trying to put a final stamp on their legacy-defining seasons, we hadJuan Soto and Mookie Betts, a suddenly rejuvenated Giancarlo Stanton and a hobbled Freddie Freeman (only raising the drama if he hit well), Gerrit Cole and Yoshinobu Yamamoto. Aside from the history between the clubs, we had both clubs needing to rewrite their recent history: The Yankees, back in the World Series for the first time since 2009, and the Dodgers trying to add a more legitimate championship to the one they won in the COVID-shortened season.
Actual World Series:C+. The Judge-Ohtani showdown was a flop, as Judge hit .222 with one home run and Ohtani hit .105 without a home run or RBI. The series also went just five games, with the Dodgers winning the first three. The series did produce two forever moments, however: Freeman's walk-off, Kirk Gibson-esque grand slam in Game 1 and the Yankees' fifth-inning defensive meltdown in Game 5.
The Red Sox were coming off their never-done-before comeback from down 3-0 to beat the Yankees in the ALCS -- and still had to beat a 105-win Cardinals team that featured Pujols (.331, 46 home runs), Jim Edmonds (.301, 42 home runs) and Scott Rolen (.314, 34 home runs), plus in-season pickup Larry Walker, who had an OPS over 1.000 that year. The Red Sox had their own ridiculous lineup with Ortiz (.301, 41 home runs), Ramirez (.308, 43 home runs) and Damon (.304, 20 home runs) plus a rotation with Schilling and Martinez. It seems inevitable now that Boston was going to win, but that wasn't the case at the time, so the buildup was intense.
Actual World Series: D. Blah. I mean, Red Sox fans will rightfully call it the best World Series ever, but after a sloppy 11-9 Game 1 played in a drizzle at Fenway (the Red Sox won despite committing four errors), the Cardinals never led again.
The Cubs had not only not won since 1908, but they hadn't even been in a World Series since 1945. The Guardians, meanwhile, had the second-longest drought of the original 16 teams, without a title since 1948. That was enough right there to build up the anticipation, but this also rates high because it was two good teams -- Chicago won 104 games while Cleveland won 94. Cubs third baseman Kris Bryant won MVP honors that year and Cleveland was led by 18-game winner Corey Kluber (who would start three times) and young rising stars Francisco Lindor and Jose Ramirez.
Actual World Series: B. The first six games weren't anything too special, but Game 7 was one of the greatest in World Series history. Cleveland tied it on Rajai Davis' three-run homer in the bottom of the eighth, the Cubs scored twice in the 10th -- following a stress-filled rain delay -- and escaped with an 8-7, curse-ending win when Cleveland had to bat little-used Michael Martinez with its season on the line.
]

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers must decide whether to offer their breakout star, Andy Pages, a new contract.
Andy Pages’ amazing 2026 season
Pages made the 2026 All-Star team after a stellar regular season, starting extremely hot and leading the team in hitting.
As the season progressed, Pages’ production cooled but stabilized at an above-average level, while his defense remained stellar all year and earned him a Gold Glove nomination.
He finished the season slashing .274/.343/.468, with a 4.5 fWAR, 15 offensive rating points above average, and 10.3 defensive rating points above average.
It was his best season by far, and his overall production was more consistent than in 2025.
In the postseason, Pages took his biggest strides. He went 7-for-26 with two walks and four RBIs, becoming one of the few players to drive in runners with men on base.
His pitch recognition, plate discipline, and vision, all of which improved during the regular season, shone in the postseason.
Pages shook off the growing perception that he would struggle in October, and now few major questions remain when analyzing the outfielder.
As he enters arbitration for the first time, the Dodgers need to decide whether to give Pages an extension.
Why the Dodgers will consider an extension
At only 25, Pages is one of the youngest players on an admittedly old team, and his defense is a major asset.
His center field play can help offset some corner weaknesses, given his range and speed.
As such a well-rounded player, Pages’ arbitration figure will keep rising, and since he has unlocked Super Two arbitration, he gets four years rather than the standard three.
In 2027 alone, MLB Trade Rumors projects Pages to earn $4.9 million.
An offseason extension could buy him out for those four years, plus some of his free-agent years, keeping him locked in for the foreseeable future.
The Dodgers did something similar with Will Smith, extending him during his second arbitration year to a 10-year, $140 million deal.
In the process, they bought out two years of arbitration and eight years of free agency.
Pages, with three years of arbitration left and entering free agency in his physical prime at 29, will cost a pretty penny as an outfielder with good contact skills and outfield defense.
A similar case is Pete Crow-Armstrong, who signed a six-year, $115 million contract this year.
The contract buys out all four of his arbitration years and two free-agent years. This deal came before his MVP-caliber season, which would have dramatically raised the deal’s value.
Uncertainty around the salary cap and what the next collective bargaining agreement could look like remains, but regardless, locking up Pages for a while may be smart business to avoid a serious rise in value, as the Cubs did.

item.title: [FanSided] Ranking Tarik Skubal suitors from favorites to dark horses
item.dc:creator: Christopher Kline
item.description: Tarik Skubal and the Los Angeles Dodgers were swept out of the NLCS by the 103-win Milwaukee Brewers, a refreshing change of pace after two years of Dodgers dominance — and a helpful reminder to the MLB owners that payroll alone does not determine winning.
